extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of moral philosophy, political theorists, legislators, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the proper method for practical arts (including morality and policy): how rules of practice should be formed, justified, and applied in relation to scientific knowledge and teleological standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Art and Science (imperative vs indicative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The imperative mood is the characteristic of art, as distinguished from science; whatever speaks in rules or precepts (ought/should) is art, while science speaks in assertions of matters of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states: 'Whatever speaks in rules, or precepts, not in assertions respecting matters of fact, is art; and ethics, or morality, is properly a portion of the art corresponding to the sciences of human nature and society.' Use this distinction to classify inquiries and determine method: rule-making problems belong to 'art' and require a different procedure than scientific description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different methods for rule-followers vs rule-makers (judge vs legislator)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agent is bound to conform to a pre-established rule (e.g., a judge under a definite written code), the method is ratiocination or syllogism; when an agent must find or construct the rule (e.g., a legislator), they must consider the reasons or grounds of the maxim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/anti-pattern: A judge 'has nothing to do with' the reasons of the law beyond interpretation; the legislator must examine grounds. The legislator who follows rules without examining reasons is 'a mere pedant'—compare the German tacticians vanquished by Napoleon as a cautionary example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of art must be grounded in scientific theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasons of a maxim of policy, or of any other rule of art, can be no other than the theorems of the corresponding science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formation of practical rules must be justified by the relevant scientific doctrines: art hands end to science; science returns a theorem about causes/conditions; art converts that theorem into a precept only after checking practicability. Treat rules as conclusions that depend on prior scientific investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art defines ends; science supplies means
rubrics_metrics.description: The art proposes to itself an end to be attained, defines the end, and hands it over to the science; science investigates causes/conditions and returns a theorem showing how the end can be produced; art then examines practicability and converts the theorem into a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This division of labor implies that deciding what ought to be aimed at (the end) is the province of practitioners/advisers of practice, whereas establishing causal relations is the task of science. Ensure clarity about which premise is normative (provided by art) and which is descriptive (provided by science).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not turn incomplete scientific theorems prematurely into precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem is not ripe for being turned into a precept until the whole of the scientific operation has been performed, including identification of all negative conditions which would prevent the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Framing a rule from partial theory risks failure when overlooked counteracting causes arise. Remedy: re-open investigation to ascertain missing conditions before promulgating a rule; if a rule fails, return to complete the scientific process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules are necessarily simplified/provisional for ordinary use
rubrics_metrics.description: For convenience, rules must often be formed from something less than an ideally perfect theory; rules of art do not attempt to comprise more conditions than require attention in ordinary cases and are therefore imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: accept that rules will abstract from rare contingencies so they remain memorable/useful. In manual arts, where conditions are few, rules may suffice alone; in complex social affairs, rely on rules only provisionally and be prepared to analyze particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constantly refer back to scientific principles in complicated affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: In complicated affairs of life and of states/societies, rules cannot be relied on without constantly referring back to the scientific laws on which they are founded to know what contingencies require modification or constitute exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wise practitioners should use rules as initial guidance but re-examine scientific grounds when circumstances permit or when a case appears unusual. Knowing the theoretical grounds helps identify when a common rule is unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deducing conduct solely from universal practical maxims (geometrical-school error)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error to deduce the line of conduct proper to particular cases from supposed universal practical maxims, overlooking the necessity of referring back to speculative science; this 'geometrical' method yields sweeping practical maxims applied as ultimate premises without checking their speculative grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: French political journalism arguing measures solely because they flow from an abstract principle (legitimacy, sovereignty) is criticized. Practical implication: check whether a practical principle rests on scientific grounds showing it produces beneficial effects, and consider trade-offs and conflicting ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art consists of rules plus necessary speculative propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: An art, or body of art, consists of the rules together with as much of the speculative propositions as comprises the justification of those rules; the complete art includes the portion of science necessary to show on what conditions the aimed effects depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or codifying an art, include not just the procedure but the relevant scientific theorems or intermediate principles that justify it, so practitioners can adapt rules when conditions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate scientific principles (generalia) are needed as bases for arts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is need of a set of intermediate scientific truths, derived from higher generalities of science, destined to serve as the generalia or first principles of the various arts (example: Monge's theory of descriptive geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendation: develop and teach these intermediate doctrines that relate available means to ends in compact, widely applicable propositions to support practical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and justification of ends is the exclusive province of Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of the end itself belongs exclusively to art and forms its peculiar province; every art has a first principle (general major premise) which asserts that the attainment of the given end is desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative decisions about what should be aimed at must be made explicitly and justified by appeal to higher principles; do not assume ends without analysis. Art must supply the initial normative premise before scientific means can be marshaled.

rubrics_metrics.name: There must be one ultimate standard for determining goodness of ends
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some standard by which to determine the goodness or badness, absolute and comparative, of ends or objects of desire; whatever that standard is, there can be but one, else conflicting approvals would require an umpire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and moral systems should adopt a coherent ultimate principle to resolve conflicts among ends. If multiple ultimate principles are posited, a higher arbitration principle becomes necessary, complicating justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate teleological standard: conduciveness to happiness (author's position)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author declares his conviction that the general principle to which all rules of practice ought to conform, and the test by which they should be tried, is that of conduciveness to the happiness of mankind, or rather, of all sentient beings; i.e., promotion of happiness is the ultimate principle of Teleology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conduciveness to happiness as the controlling test for ends and rules of action. Note the author’s nuance: this is a justification and controller of ends, not necessarily the sole immediate end in every act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as controller but not sole immediate end; allow for higher virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotion of happiness should be the controller of ends but is not itself necessarily the sole immediate end; some virtuous actions may sacrifice immediate happiness if they can be justified by producing greater overall happiness or cultivating dispositions that increase happiness in the long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or prescribing rules, allow for the legitimacy of actions that reduce immediate pleasure when they demonstrably serve a broader teleological account (e.g., cultivating character) that ultimately promotes more happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish descriptive science from normative advising (scientist vs adviser roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific observer or reasoner, merely as such, is not an adviser for practice; his part is only to show consequences from causes and means; whether the ends themselves ought to be pursued is not part of his business as a cultivator of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the category error of letting scientific description substitute for normative justification. Practitioners must invoke teleological doctrine to decide ends; scientists should not unilaterally make normative claims without that framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rules when necessary but modify when exceptional circumstances occur
rubrics_metrics.description: By a wise practitioner, rules of conduct will only be considered as provisional; they point out the least perilous action in ordinary cases where time or means do not exist for full analysis; if unsuitable to the case, the reason will likely stem from some unusual circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational rule: apply rules for expediency when analysis is impossible; but when time/resources allow, perform the scientific process relative to the particular case and revise the rule accordingly. Treat rules as admonitions, not absolute mandates.
